newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy CPI will have difficulty falling more - Istat.
newsitem.headline: Italy CPI will have difficulty falling more - Istat.

text.p: Italian inflation will struggle to maintain the downward momentum achieved in 1996, the head of national statistics institute Istat told parliament on Thursday.
Alberto Zuliani told the lower house's budget committee that inflation would benefit from the knock-on impact of last year's strong decline in the consumer price index.

"But it will have difficulty taking advantage of the effects of any further lira appreciations or a containment in real-terms of salaries," he said, adding that companies could not be expected to absorb any rise in the cost of raw materials.
Inflation fell to 2.4 percent year-on-year in February, its lowest level for more than a quarter of a century.
Zuliani added that the benefits from cuts last year in utility tariffs would begin to drop out of the system in the second half of 1997.
The government has forecast average annual inflation of 2.5 percent in 1997 from 3.9 percent in 1996.
Turning to economic growth, Zuliani said indications of slow industrial output at the start of the year may have a negative impact on gross domestic product (GDP) in the first quarter.
He said preliminary data pointed to seasonally adjusted industrial production slipping 0.8 percent in the first quarter of 1997 by comparison with the final three months of 1996.
However, if the number of working days was taken into account, production rose an adjusted 1.5 percent.

"From this scenario there therefore emerges a possible negative impact on GDP growth in the first quarter," Zuliani said, adding that this might be partially counterbalanced by the fact that the investment goods component of GDP was set to climb 4.7 percent quarter-on-quarter between January and March.

State economic research body Isco told the committee that it expected GDP growth to hit 1.7 percent in 1997 after 0.8 percent growth in 1996. The Bank of Italy said last month it expected growth this year to be close to 1996 levels. -- Rome newsroom +396 678 2501
